papers.title: How wide must an eavesdropper be? Leakage of a toric-code logical bit to a strip and the Nishimori point
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computers hand pieces of each logical qubit to separate decoder modules and shared readout lines. How much does a piece reveal? We prove that for any region and any Pauli noise, including correlated noise, an observer's optimal advantage in learning a logical bit is exactly 1 - 2 P_fail, where P_fail is the failure probability of maximum-likelihood decoding confined to that region. Two lessons follow. Geometry, not noise, provides the protection: a region that misses a single column of the code learns exactly nothing at any noise level, while a region that spans the code is protected by noise only at impractical distances (d > 350 for one row at a 10^-3 flip rate). And width is a poor guide to risk: under i.i.d. noise a two-row strip learns exactly as little as one row, yet below threshold an eavesdropper needs a width growing only as ln d. Through the identity, the strip's operational threshold is the Nishimori point of the random-bond Ising model, and a Walsh-Hadamard transfer matrix up to width 16 locates it to within a few thousandths. On two IBM Heron processors (d = 3, 5), an emulated strip adversary shows the predicted jump at width three, and non-uniform qubit errors let a trained attacker profit from the second row that uniform noise makes useless. We turn these results into design rules for partitioned decoding and multiplexed readout. Code and data are included.

papers.title: Computational Power of Clifford and Ising Quantum Computers
papers.abstract: We extend the efficient classical simulation of Ising quantum computers from braidings to measurements. We investigate several different definitions of efficient Clifford quantum computation by varying the power of the circuit generator. In case the circuit generator can see the entire input, we give a detailed proof that efficient simulation of classical computation would imply the separation of complexity classes $\mathbf{P}$ and $\mathbf{PSPACE}$. If the circuit generator sees only the input length, we prove that Clifford quantum computers decide what we call affine languages.

papers.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
papers.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.

papers.title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
papers.abstract: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits ($1.2 \times 10^8$ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)$_3$-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

papers.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
papers.abstract: Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

papers.title: Computational complexity of Berry phase estimation in topological phases of matter
papers.abstract: The Berry phase is a fundamental quantity in the classification of topological phases of matter. In this paper, we present a new quantum algorithm and several complexity-theoretical results for the Berry phase estimation (BPE) problems. Our new quantum algorithm achieves BPE in a more general setting than previously known quantum algorithms, with a theoretical guarantee. For the complexity-theoretic results, we consider two main cases. First, we prove $\mathsf{BQP}$-completeness when we are given a guiding state that has a large overlap with the ground state. This result establishes an exponential quantum speedup for estimating the Berry phase. Second, we prove $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$-completeness when we have an $\textit{a priori}$ bound for the ground-state energy. Here, $\mathsf{UQMA}$ is the unique witness version of $\mathsf{QMA}$, and $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$ precisely captures the complexity of BPE without the known guiding state. Remarkably, this problem is, to our knowledge, the first natural problem complete for $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$. These results advance the role of quantum computing in the study of topological phases of matter and provide a pathway for clarifying the connection between topological phases of matter and computational complexity.

papers.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
papers.abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every nonlinearity is a quadratic detection (an interference, a balanced interferometric reading or a camera) and the output is a Born probability: attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^2$, the form of the Born rule, normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout; between detections a classical controller squares, divides, rescales and re-encodes. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-13}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference the model reaches 77.45 +- 0.91 % test accuracy, level within the spread of three seeds with a softmax transformer of the same size (76.62 +- 0.36 %). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 44 % of test pairs, out of the 53 % any single deletion can change, against 32 % for the softmax model's integrated gradients and 31 % for the Born Transformer's own attention. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics (simulated), and its attention overlaps to Hadamard tests on qubits; a separate coherent attention layer becomes one post-selected circuit (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps, the device gave the model's answers on the two shortest test pairs, also when the one word that decides one of them was deleted; with calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence on one pair (correlation 0.997) and on the other less closely (0.962).

papers.title: Beyond the Mean Gap: What Transferred-Angle QAOA Retains on a Superconducting Processor
papers.abstract: Hardware executions of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) are often validated by comparing the device's mean cost with a simulation, a check that can miss what matters for optimization. Under global depolarization, the mean normalized gap and the floor-corrected probability of every set of bitstrings, the optimum included, retain the same fraction of their noiseless improvement over uniform sampling. We test this prediction with depth-2, transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition on the IBM Heron processor \texttt{ibm\_marrakesh}, with and without dynamical decoupling and twirling. At 12 qubits, the main-family circuits retained 29\% to 46\% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5\% to 15\% of their probability of the optimum, lower on at least nine of ten instances per run. Near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, whereas the avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. In the first submission, a device-matched noise model reproduced the pattern but overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold. On a rugged planted family, the device found the optimum in 62\% of 768-shot blocks (noiseless: 98\%), within the range of local heuristics. Validations of optimization circuits should report retention of the optimum and of near-optimal sets.

papers.title: Polynomial Quantum Recurrent Channels for Matrix Inverse Actions: Deferred-Reset Dynamics and Chebyshev Filtering
papers.abstract: We develop completely positive, trace-preserving polynomial recurrent channels for quantum solution-state preparation and derive fixed-point and time-varying tracking bounds. Across 2,880 synthetic configurations, resident Chebyshev recurrence improves accuracy-passing snapshot counts in 608 cases, ties in 2,271, and loses in one. A separate 360-scenario cost study shows that fresh recurrence is cheaper in all 184 jointly feasible scenarios (median resident-to-fresh cost ratio: 3.12), while resident recurrence uniquely satisfies accuracy requirements in 74 cases. At a logical noise rate of $10^-4$, neither recurrent method qualifies. Based on exact reduced-density simulations and assumed cost models, our results demonstrate conditional tracking advantages but no general end-to-end speedup or total-cost benefit.

papers.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
papers.abstract: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

papers.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
papers.abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a $12$-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of $0.969$. The query consumes $3.51\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{J}$ of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of $4.38\,\mathrm{W}$ and a peak of $64.4\,\mathrm{W}$. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

papers.title: A New Quantum Linear System Algorithm Beyond the Condition Number and Its Application to Solving Multivariate Polynomial Systems
papers.abstract: Given a matrix $A$ of dimension $M \times N$ and a vector $\vec{b}$, the quantum linear system (QLS) problem asks for the preparation of a quantum state $|\vec{y}\rangle$ proportional to the solution of $A\vec{y} = \vec{b}$. Existing QLS algorithms have runtimes that scale linearly with the condition number $\kappa(A)$, the sparsity of $A$, and logarithmically with inverse precision, but often overlook structural properties of $\vec{b}$, whose alignment with $A$'s eigenspaces can greatly affect performance. In this work, we present a new QLS algorithm that explicitly leverages the structure of the right-hand side vector $\vec{b}$. The runtime of our algorithm depends polynomially on the sparsity of the augmented matrix $H = [A, -\vec{b}]$, the inverse precision, the $\ell_2$ norm of the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$, and a new instance-dependent parameter \[ ET= \sum_{i=1}^M p_i^2 \cdot d_i, \] where $\vec{p} = (AA^{\top})^+ \vec{b}$, and $d_i$ denotes the squared $\ell_2$ norm of the $i$-th row of $H$. We also introduce a structure-aware rescaling technique tailored to the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$. Unlike left preconditioning methods, which transform the linear system to $DA\vec{y} = D\vec{b}$, our approach applies a right rescaling matrix, reformulating the linear system as $AD\vec{z} = \vec{b}$. As an application of our instance-aware QLS algorithm and new rescaling scheme, we develop a quantum algorithm for solving multivariate polynomial systems in regimes where prior QLS-based methods fail. This yields an end-to-end framework applicable to a broad class of problems. In particular, we apply it to the maximum independent set (MIS) problem, formulated as a special case of a polynomial system, and show through detailed analysis that, under certain conditions, our quantum algorithm for MIS runs in polynomial time.

papers.title: Pauli-Z Moment Matrices in the Variational Quantum Power Method: Goemans-Williamson Rounding, Qubit Locking, and a Correlation-Based Circuit-Cutting Heuristic
papers.abstract: The matrix of single- and two-qubit Pauli-Z expectation values of any quantum state is the moment matrix of its computational-basis outcome distribution; it therefore lies in the cut polytope and, in particular, is a feasible point of the degree-2 Sum-of-Squares (Goemans-Williamson, GW) relaxation. Applying GW random-hyperplane rounding to this matrix yields cuts of expected weight at least alpha_GW times the state's energy. This observation and the resulting bound are not new: the bound is the GW inequality applied to the circuit's covariance matrix, and it was stated and used in exactly this form by Martinez, Fawzi and Stilck Franca, who interpret it as showing that a classical surrogate nearly reproduces the circuit and add noisy-circuit guarantees and hardware experiments; relax-and-round of QAOA correlation matrices, with spectral rather than hyperplane rounding, was introduced earlier by Dupont and Sundar. The bound is also not stronger than what direct computational-basis sampling of the state already gives in expectation. In this note we revisit the bound as a post-processing of the two-point data produced by variational algorithms such as QAOA and the Variational Quantum Power Method (VQPM), and give an energy-leakage bound for VQPM qubit locking. We further discuss a heuristic that uses the connected Z-correlation matrix to propose candidate qubit bipartitions for circuit cutting, in the spirit of existing correlation- and mutual-information-based partitioning methods, together with product-state error bounds in terms of quantum mutual information. Pairwise Z-correlations neither certify product structure of the state nor factorization of the underlying unitary, and the error bounds require quantities not available from Z-data alone.

papers.title: Asymmetric quantum error correction efficiently tackles application-specific noise effects
papers.abstract: Noise is a major challenge for current quantum computers. It can be broadly categorized into bit-flip and phase-flip errors. These two types do not necessarily affect the executed algorithm, thus also the application, in the same way. We illustrate this general effect for the example of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) applied to a small instance of the flight-gate assignment (FGA) problem. We compare bit-flip and phase-flip Pauli noise under both layer-level and gate-level noise models, using two circuit decompositions of the same ideal QAOA unitary: a CNOT-based decomposition and a native-RZZ decomposition. For the six-qubit FGA instance considered here, bit-flip noise produces a larger degradation in the optimized QAOA performance across the investigated circuit depths and noise models. The asymmetry is most pronounced in the layer-level and native-RZZ simulations. We explain this behavior through the commutation and propagation properties of the errors and their effects on the final computational-basis measurements. Since these mechanisms are not specific to the considered FGA instance, we expect similar noise asymmetries to arise in other Ising-based QAOA applications, although this remains to be investigated. We then exploit these insights to tackle noise particularly efficiently using asymmetric error-correcting codes. As an illustration, we use the quantum parity code (QPC), a generalization of the 9-qubit Shor code, and show that a smaller asymmetric code can achieve nearly the same improvement as a larger symmetric choice. This suggests that allocating error-correction resources according to algorithmic noise sensitivity, rather than physical error rates alone, can be beneficial even when the physical noise is symmetric. Finally, we discuss how information about the noise obtained through calibration can be exploited in our approach.

papers.title: Alchemically Transferable Parameters for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
papers.abstract: Machine-learned circuit parameters could remove one of the main bottlenecks of variational quantum eigensolvers: the classical optimization loop, with its typical barren plateaus, local minima, and costly energy and gradient evaluations, is replaced by a direct prediction. Prior work showed that machine-learning models paired with a structured circuit design can transfer across system size and structure within hydrogenic systems. The next step: Extending them to organic molecules would seem to require re-training on use-case-specific training sets. In this work, we show that this is not necessary by establishing an alchemical approach. A geometric projection places surrogate hydrogen atoms along the bond directions of the target molecule and so maps its local bonding environment onto small hydrogenic fragments. Existing hydrogenic solvers can then be reused as they are. The only new quantity is a single projection radius per bond type, which is fitted once on a small reference molecule and reused unchanged thereafter. We demonstrate the approach on the separable-pair circuit designs that have been used in prior work and extend the approach to multi-circuit approaches that span effective bases for quantum subspaces.

papers.title: Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM): A Unified Learning-Based Framework for Noise Resilience in Quantum Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Error mitigation stands between variational quantum algorithms and useful results on today's noisy hardware, yet in practice a mitigation method is usually chosen once, by hand, and applied unchanged for the life of an experiment. This is a poor fit for quantum machine learning (QML), where the circuit and the noise drift as training proceeds, so the best strategy in one regime is often wrong in another. We present a generalized form of Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM), which treats the choice of mitigation technique as an online decision made from an algorithm's own feedback. A single contextual-bandit controller observes signals any variational algorithm already produces, such as fidelity, entropy, reward or loss, and gradient behavior, and selects among Zero-Noise Extrapolation, Probabilistic Error Cancellation, Measurement Error Mitigation, Dynamical Decoupling, and circuit optimization per step. Because it depends only on this shared feedback interface, the framework applies unchanged across supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, and hybrid quantum-classical learning. Evaluated on five paradigms across 80 algorithm-and-noise conditions, adaptive selection reaches 95.5% of an oracle that always picks the best technique and significantly outperforms all six fixed strategies (Friedman $\chi^{2}=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$; pairwise Wilcoxon $p<4\times10^{-6}$). The learned policy is noise-aware: its favored technique shifts as depolarizing and readout error rise. On noise models from eight real IBM devices, APGEM tracks the oracle almost exactly (99.9% of oracle utility) at a flat cost of roughly $1.3\times10^{4}$ shots from three to eight qubits.

papers.title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
papers.abstract: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

papers.title: Parametric Proof-Carrying Compilation for Quantum Error-Correction
papers.abstract: We present PC-QEC, a proof-carrying compilation framework for quantum error correction parameterized by both code distance and syndrome-extraction scheme. It covers all four schemes---Standard, Flag, Shor and Knill---with circuit-level distance guarantees for every legal code distance in each proved family under the declared fault and readout contracts. The circuit-level model permits single-wire Pauli faults at every operation's qubit operands, capturing data errors, readout errors and ancilla faults that propagate into multi-qubit hook errors. For each family and scheme, code-algebra proofs and fault-aware Hoare proofs compose into a finite symbolic certificate whose size is independent of code distance. We demonstrate family-wide guarantees for five code families across all four schemes. For rotated Surface code, one Standard Scheme certificate proves a distance lower bound $d$ for every odd $d\ge3$ and checks in 214\,s on average. Lean 4 mechanizes the metatheory and exact circuit-level distances for canonical Surface, hypergraph-product (HGP) and Toric code families.

papers.title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
papers.abstract: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.

papers.title: Second-level termination of the PPT entanglement-cost hierarchy for two qutrits
papers.abstract: We prove that for arbitrary two-qutrit quantum states, the semidefinite programming lower-bound hierarchy for the PPT entanglement cost terminates at the second level. Therefore, under operations preserving positive partial transpose, its zero-error asymptotic entanglement cost can be obtained by a semidefinite program involving only three Hermitian matrix variables. The key to the proof is to shorten the feasible dual chain by one level; to this end, we combine finite certificates verified by exact rational arithmetic with analytic estimates near the boundary of the parameter domain. This result shows that a unified terminating level exists for two-qutrit systems, whereas no unified terminating level exists for all dimensions.

papers.title: The wave equation and two-electron atomic wavefunctions
papers.abstract: Axisymmetric solutions of the classical wave equation in three spatial dimensions are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence to functions which annihilate the two-electron kinetic energy operator expressed in coordinates relative to a fixed nucleus.

papers.title: Sample complexity of learning fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states with single-copy and entangled measurements
papers.abstract: With single-copy measurements, every mixed fermionic Gaussian state on $m$ modes, pure modes included, is learned to trace distance $\epsilon$ from $\Theta(m^3/\epsilon^2)$ copies, with no logarithmic factor, against the known $\Theta(m^2/\epsilon^2)$ for collective measurements. We prove the upper bound, resolving Conjecture 10.1 of arXiv:2609.23189 (lower bound for $\epsilon\le1/3600$), and fill most open entries of the sample-complexity table of fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states, for single-copy, $k$-copy and collective measurements. The single-copy measurement's noise is matched to the metric at every occupation scale. With blocks of $k$ copies, the covariant highest-weight measurement of arXiv:2611.07271, read out through the Weyl-shift estimator, is exactly unbiased for every state; it gives $\Theta(\max\{m^3/k,m^2\}/\epsilon^2)$ in Frobenius norm on all states and in trace distance on every class at a fixed distance from the pure boundary. The gain $1/k$ ($k\le m$) away from the pure boundary, against $1/\sqrt k$ on cold number-conserving states, is therefore attained. For bosonic Gaussian states with bounded covariance, any displacement and squeezing, and occupations $n_1\le\dots\le n_m$, $O((m^2+r^3+\sum_{i,j>r}1/(n_i+n_j))/\epsilon^2)$ single-copy measurements suffice, $r$ the largest index with $r\,n_r\le2$; this is the minimax rate on dyadic-interval classes, with no spectral gap or cold-mode count assumed, and holds with no covariance bound for displaced passive states. With no bound on energy or squeezing, non-Gaussian measurements learn centred one-mode states, mixed included, from $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ and centred pure $m$-mode states from $O(m^2/\epsilon^2)$ single copies, free of the $\log\log E$ term of Gaussian measurements, and $m$-mode states from $O(m^3/\epsilon^2)$ copies, entangled only in a first round on blocks of $4m+6$.

papers.title: Maximal Violation of Mermin Inequality for Commuting von Neumann Algebras and Multipartite Vacuum Entanglement in QFT
papers.abstract: Summers and Werner proved that Bell inequalities are violated maximally and generically in the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory in [S. J. Summers and R. Werner, Commun. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 247-259]. Their criterion concerns two-party case, that is, there are two algebras of quantum observables: one algebra and its commutant. In this case, the maximal CHSH value is converged to in every normal state exactly when the algebra is strongly stable. In the paper, we study the corresponding question for three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras. We focus on the multipartite Mermin inequalities instead of CHSH ones. For the tripartite Mermin functional we show that maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is an necessary condition for maximal violation, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of the individual algebras, even together with tripartite duality, do not suffice to arrive at the maximal violation. The results are also extended to n>=3 parties.

papers.title: CV-TF-QKD
papers.abstract: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrt{\eta}$, where $\eta$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.

papers.title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
papers.abstract: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is the presence of crosstalk that complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate experimentally our approach using a single NV center as well as superconducting transmons. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

papers.title: Quantum Oracle Value Readout: Coherence, Complementarity, and Fragility
papers.abstract: A response-register quantum oracle can reveal a function value or encode it as a phase through kickback. We quantify how much value information can be recovered from one query at a fixed fidelity to a target phase character, and how noise and implementation errors affect readout performance. For pure response states over finite Abelian groups, the known covariant discrimination solution fixes the optimal readout probability exactly in terms of the $\ell_1$-norm coherence of the response state in the character basis. Using a known coherence bound, we determine the complete pure-state readout interval at fixed target-character fidelity. Discarding the response leaves a mixture of phase-oracle channels whose distance from the target, measured by half the diamond norm, is at most the target-character infidelity, with equality for surjective functions. We then identify when coherence alone determines performance and when apparatus correlations or loss profiles are also needed. For coherent analyzer errors, we derive the full quadratic loss and an exact scalar reduction of the profile model on the upper phase--value boundary. For mode-dependent loss, no-detection events can carry value information, and a universal bound is attained under a phase--loss compatibility condition. Photonic-mesh simulations test the analyzer-error predictions, with the controlled oracle itself assumed. Selected results extend to finite non-Abelian groups, where scalar phase kickback is restricted to one-dimensional representations.

papers.title: A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
papers.abstract: Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.

papers.title: Lorentzian entropy, subgaussian matrix concentration, and sharp functional inequalities for all matroids
papers.abstract: We prove complete entropy contraction for homogeneous Lorentzian laws and derive subgaussian matrix concentration and sharp functional inequalities for every matroid. Uniform retention of $\ell$ out of $r$ particles contracts matrix entropy by the optimal universal factor $\ell/r$, in every finite matrix dimension and positive field, including repeated labels. The matrix Laplace comparison retains matrix variance and arbitrary Hermitian offsets. It gives subgaussian bounds for arbitrary Hermitian observables with bounded exchange differences, and Chernoff and Bernstein bounds for basis sums. Every unit-edge matroid basis graph satisfies the cube's small-set and Gross inequalities, with equality classified and optimal universal complete entropy-decay rate four. Its spectrum lies in $\{0,2\}\cup[3,\infty)$, with binary direct-factor contrasts spanning the eigenspace at two. We classify extremal down-up eigenfunctions, resolving Alaniz Pintos's degree-one conjecture and the equality problem for the Feder--Mihail walk. For degree at least two, every matrix entropy extremizer extends uniquely from its two-particle marginal. Equality depends only on the normalized pair law, with noncommutativity confined to mutually exclusive labels. We classify power-entropy extremizers for $1<p<2$ and give a fourth-order criterion for affine equality. Retained-level Gibbs reconstruction has sharp dimension-independent stability. For multiaffine laws whose generating polynomial and complement are Lorentzian, we determine the exact simultaneous all-field quantum marginal and matrix H\"older regions and classify the sharp half-marginal fields. Connected sharp laws are determinantal through rank three; stable nondeterminantal examples exist in every higher rank.

papers.title: Universal Fold Caustics in Anharmonic Matter-wave Lenses
papers.abstract: Caustics provide a universal connection between classical ray focusing and structured wave patterns. We theoretically investigate this connection in non-linear matter waves focused by a short-duration anharmonic lens acting on a Bose-Einstein condensate. A semi-classical description shows how the leading cubic aberration transforms the harmonic focal point into a fold caustic, whose local wave field is described by an Airy canonical integral. Three-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii simulations show that mean-field interactions modify the near-focus density and longitudinal momentum distribution, producing a secondary momentum-space feature absent from the non-interacting evolution. We quantify the information about the effective interaction strength carried by the $1D$ distribution using classical Fisher information and maximum-likelihood estimation. We obtain a relative uncertainty of $2.7\times10^{-3}$ for a sample of $10^5$ detected points along $z$. These results establish a framework for studying interaction-driven departures from single-particle caustic universality and promote matter-wave lenses as a sensitive probe of mean-field interactions.

papers.title: Neutron Scattering studies of the density dependence of One-dimensional Quantum Fluids
papers.abstract: In previous work, we demonstrated that $^4$He confined within a templated porous material preplated with a noble gas to enhance dimensional reduction exhibits one-dimensional behavior. Neutron scattering revealed that the excitations in confined $^4$He are qualitatively distinct from those in two- and three-dimensional superfluid helium, aligning with quantum Monte Carlo calculations. These simulations suggest that three solid layers form, with a one-dimensional liquid located at the center of the pore. Here, we present neutron scattering results as the filling fraction of the one-dimensional core is varied. We observe that the one-dimensional liquid always forms with a fixed density, even as the pore filling increases. We posit that this is due to the growth of the one dimensional extent of the liquid as the filling is increased, but its density remains unchanged.
